programs.name: Industrial Engineering BS
notes: 3 general technical elective courses chosen from areas below

courses.title: Why IE: Professional Foundations of Industrial Engineering
courses.desc: In this seminar course we introduce first- and second-year students to the field of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences (IEMS) and its ethical, global and societal contexts. Focus on modeling, systems thinking and process improvement, as well as the career paths of IE graduates. Opportunities will be provided to develop skills in teamwork and in oral and written communication.
courses.text: Prerequisite: Open only to first- and second-year students.

courses.title: Introduction to Statistics
courses.desc: Collecting data; summarizing and displaying data; drawing conclusions from data; probability background, confidence intervals, hypotheses tests, regression, correlation. Not open to industrial engineering degree candidates. May not receive credit for both IEMS 201-0 and any of BMD_ENG 220-0, IEMS 303-0, or CHEM_ENG 312-0.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 218-2 or MATH 220-2 or equivalent.

courses.title: Principles of Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: Introduction to essential elements of building one's own business, from brainstorming ideas and assessing opportunities to pitching a business idea. History of entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial psyche. Business plan fundamentals, including strategy, finance, accounting, marketing, operations, and choosing the ideal management team. Taught with ENTREP 225-0; may not receive credit for both courses. May not be taken after IEMS 325-0 or ENTREP 325-0.

courses.title: Professional Practice Studio
courses.desc: This course develops the professional and analytical skills required for successful industrial engineering project work. Students learn how to scope problems, conduct relevant background research, select appropriate models and methods, perform simple analysis, and communicate results through clear writing, effective visualizations, and compelling narratives. The class will use many short cases and applied exercises to teach concepts.?No previous?IE courses are required.?The course is meant to prepare students for internships, the?Client Project Challenge (CPC) class, other IE classes, and their careers.
courses.text: Prerequisites: DSGN 106-1 , DSGN 106-2 , sophomore standing.

courses.title: Introduction to Statistical Learning
courses.desc: This course offers a modern treatment of statistical learning, focusing on modeling data for prediction and insight. It blends theoretical foundations with practical programming applications to prepare students for both advanced study and real-world data analysis. May not receive credit for both IEMS 301-0 and IEMS 304-0.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 201-0 , IEMS 303-0 ,BMD_ENG 220-0, CHEM_ENG 312-0 , GEN_ENG 231-0 , or MATH 314-0 ; COMP_SCI 110-0 , COMP_SCI 150-0 , GEN_ENG 150-0 , GEN_ENG 151-0 , GEN_ENG 205-1 , or GEN_ENG 206-1 ; GEN_ENG 241-0 .

courses.title: Probability
courses.desc: Introduction to probability theory and its applications. Conditional probabilities and expectation values. Random variables and distributions, including binomial, Poisson, exponential, and normal. Joint distributions and limit laws for foundation of and connection to statistics. Examples in reliability, inventory, finance, and statistics. May not receive credit for both IEMS 302-0 and any of the following: ELEC_ENG 302-0; MATH 310-1, MATH 314-0, MATH 385-0; STAT 320-1, STAT 383-0.
courses.text: Prerequisite: prior completion of or concurrent enrollment in MATH 228-2 .

courses.title: Engineering Statistics
courses.desc: A second course in statistics that goes deeper into estimation theory and nonparametric statistics, and introduces Bayesian inference, experiment design and ANOVA.
courses.text: Prerequisite: IEMS 302-0 or equivalent.

courses.title: Statistical Learning for Data Analysis
courses.desc: Predictive modeling of data using modern regression and classification methods. Multiple linear regression; logistic regression; pitfalls and diagnostics; nonparametric and nonlinear regression and classification such as trees, nearest neighbors, neural networks, and ensemble methods.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 303-0 or equivalent.

courses.title: Foundations of Modern Machine Learning
courses.desc: This course introduces the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of machine learning methods, with an emphasis on modern algorithmic developments. The curriculum spans classical statistical learning techniques including regression, classification, regularization, and clustering as well as contemporary deep learning architectures such as feedforward and convolutional neural networks, recurrent models, and transformers. Core algorithmic principles, including backpropagation, optimization, regularization, and representation learning, are developed both analytically and through software implementation. Students engage with the material through coding-based projects and by examining the computational foundations of large-scale language models.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 301-0 or IEMS 304-0 or equivalent.

courses.title: Quality Improvement by Experimental Design
courses.desc: Methods for designing and analyzing industrial experiments. Blocking; randomization; multiple regression; factorial and fractional factorial experiments; response surface methodology; Taguchi's robust design; split plot experimentation. Homework, labs, and project.
courses.text: Prerequisite: IEMS 201-0 , IEMS 303-0 , or equivalent.

courses.title: Operations Research
courses.desc: Survey of operations research techniques. Linear programming, decision theory, stochastic processes, game theory. May not be taken for credit with or after IEMS 313-0.
courses.text: Prerequisites: GEN_ENG 205-1 , GEN_ENG 206-1 or MATH 240-0 or GEN_ENG 150-0 or GEN_ENG 151-0 ; GEN_ENG 241-0 .

courses.title: Linear Optimization for Decision Making
courses.desc: Formulation and solution of applicable optimization models, including linear, integer, nonlinear, and network problems. Efficient algorithmic methods and use of computer modeling languages and systems. Homework, exams, and project.
courses.text: Prerequisites: COMP_SCI 110-0 , COMP_SCI 111-0 , or COMP_SCI 150-0 ; GEN_ENG 205-1 , GEN_ENG 206-1 , GEN_ENG 150-0 or GEN_ENG 151-0 ; GEN_ENG 241-0 ; MATH 228-1 ; sophomore standing .

courses.title: Nonlinear Optimization for Decision Making
courses.desc: Theory and algorithms of nonlinear optimization as a bridge between deterministic linear models and data-driven decision making under uncertainty. This course covers convex and nonconvex modeling, first- and second-order optimality conditions, duality theory, and numerical methods including gradient-based, stochastic, Newton-type, and constrained optimization algorithms. Case studies from machine learning, finance, and engineering motivate the formulation and analysis of real-world nonlinear models. Students implement foundational solvers from first principles, construct more advanced solvers using generative-AI assisted development, and deploy these methods on applications such as nonlinear regression and classification, portfolio optimization, and parameter estimation in complex systems.
courses.text: Prerequisites: GEN_ENG 150 or COMP_SCI 150, GEN_ENG 231, GEN_ENG 241, MATH 228-1 ; or equivalent.

courses.title: Stochastic Models
courses.desc: Fundamental concepts of probability theory; modeling and analysis of systems having random dynamics, particularly queueing systems.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 302-0 ; GEN_ENG 205-1 , GEN_ENG 206-1 , GEN_ENG 150-0 or GEN_ENG 151-0 ; GEN_ENG 241-0 ; ES_APPM 245-0 ; and prior completion of or concurrent enrollment in IEMS 303-0 .

courses.title: Discrete Event Systems Simulation
courses.desc: Computer simulation of discrete-change systems subject to uncertainty. Choice of input distributions; development of models; design and analysis of simulation experiments. Mini-projects, exams, and computer labs.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 303-0 ; IEMS 310-0 or IEMS 315-0 .

courses.title: Engineering Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: Overview of the entrepreneurial process from an engineering perspective. Idea generation, planning, financing, marketing, protecting, staffing, leading, growing, and harvesting. Business models for startups. Lectures, guest speakers, and case studies. Taught with IEMS 325-0; may not receive credit for both courses.
courses.text: Prerequisite: 1 course in accounting or finance such as CIV_ENV 205-0 or ENTREP 330-1 .

courses.title: Qualitative Methods in Engineering Systems
courses.desc: Use of field research methods to solve management problems. Students define projects, design field studies and pilot tests of data collection instruments, and present results.
courses.text: Prerequisites: DSGN 106-1 and DSGN 106-2 , or consent of instructor for non-McCormick students.

courses.title: Social Networks Analysis
courses.desc: The use of social network analysis to understand the growing connectivity and complexity in the world around us on different scales, ranging from small groups to the World Wide Web. How we create social, economic, and technological networks, and how they enable and constrain attitudes and behaviors.

courses.title: Organizational Behavior
courses.desc: Manager's view of tools available to recruit, develop, appraise, compensate, organize, and lead a team going through change. Application of psychological principles relating to human dynamics, motivation, teams, power, and organizational culture. Lectures, guest speakers, and exams. Work experience recommended.

courses.title: Project Management for Engineers
courses.desc: A case study-based exploration of the body of project management knowledge. Key topics include project scheduling, risk management, project leadership, small-group dynamics, project methodologies, lifecycle concepts, and project controls. A Socratic approach is taken to exploring various case studies in the context of established and leading-edge project management concepts.
courses.text: Prerequisites: CIV_ENV 205-0 and IEMS 303-0 .

courses.title: Whole-Brain Leadership
courses.desc: This course examines whole-brain thinking and leading. Students will draw upon previous work and leadership experience to identify their own thinking and leading preferences and those of team member, and will examine contrasting thinking and leading styles in an effort to appreciate and combine these to produce optimal outcomes. A number of leadership theories and ways of leading will be examined including creative and agile leadership. Analytical thinkers/leaders will be challenged to spend more time with innovation and creativity, while creative thinkers/leaders will be presented with opportunities to engage in analytical problem-solving. Work experience recommended.
courses.text: Prerequisite: Junior standing.

courses.title: Negotiations and Conflict Resolution for Engineers
courses.desc: In this highly interactive class, students participate in negotiation and dispute resolution simulations that range in complexity from single-party/single-issue to multiparty/ multi-issue cases. In addition students explore the role of agents and third parties in the managing conflict. Throughout all of the simulations integrative and distributive strategies are emphasized that can be applied across a variety of contexts.
courses.text: Prerequisite: Junior standing.

courses.title: Organizational Leadership
courses.desc: This course enables students to think critically about leadership in organizations by understanding five facets of leadership. The five facets are areas of theorizing that explain what makes leadership effective: features, functions, form, fit, and focus. We will learn to answer questions about who is influential, what makes for good leadership, when (under what conditions?), and why (through what mechanisms?) is leadership successful. We explore leadership concepts using a set of illustrative case studies of interesting people who have led interesting lives of impact. Students may not receive credit for both IEMS 349-0 and COMM_ST 350-SA.

courses.title: Humans, AI, and the Future of Decision-making
courses.desc: Examines how individuals, teams, and organizations make decisions alongside AI systems. Students develop diagnostic tools to identify where AI adds value, choose appropriate integration strategies, and design the role, process, and governance changes that transformative AI adoption requires. Drawing on management research and practice, the course prepares students to lead AI-enabled change across levels of analysis, from individual workflows to organizational transformation.

courses.title: AI-Enabled Sequential Decision Making
courses.desc: Formulation and solution of sequential decision-making problems under uncertainty. Markov decision processes and exact solution methods, including value iteration, policy iteration, and linear programming. Model-based methods, including model predictive control and Monte Carlo tree search. Model-free reinforcement learning methods, including deep Q networks, policy gradient, and actorcritic algorithms. Students implement these methods in Python and apply them through case studies that highlight the capabilities and limitations of each approach.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 303-0 , IEMS 313-0 , IEMS 314-0 .

courses.title: Foundations of Generative AI & Reasoning Systems
courses.desc: This course provides a hands-on introduction to the science and algorithms behind today’s Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic AI. Architecture, training, and deployment of transformer-based models. Prompt engineering (including algorithmic approaches), and post-training with reinforcement learning methods such as RLHF and direct preference optimization for alignment and safety. The course also covers large reasoning models, in-context learning, and agentic AI state-of-the-art (architectures, memory, context engineering). Focus on practical implementations using modern software techniques and understanding the science of LLMs and agents.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 304-0 , COMP_SCI 217-0 .

courses.title: Analytics for Social Good
courses.desc: Challenges and opportunities in using analytics to pursue social good. Application of data-analysis and decision-making tools and frameworks to such case studies as disaster response and community-based healthcare. For juniors and seniors with interests in humanitarian and nonprofit operations.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 303-0 and IEMS 313-0 .

courses.title: Tech Investment & Enterprise Strategy
courses.desc: Examines how investors and executives evaluate, raise capital, and compete around technology-driven businesses. Emphasizes how valuation frameworks must be adapted to account for uncertainty, scalability, competitive dynamics, and strategic interaction. Covers fundamentals of technology valuation and investing, spanning venture capital, growth equity, and private equity contexts; and examination of how strategy shapes value, introducing tools such as network effects, strategy rules, competitive tactics, and reasoning under deep technological uncertainty. Throughout the course, students integrate financial analysis with strategic judgment through discussion of real-world cases.
courses.text: Prerequisites: CIV_ENV 205-0 or equivalent.

courses.title: Intro to Financial Engineering
courses.desc: Financial markets, derivative securities, risk management, mathematical models in finance. Foreign exchange, debt, equity, commodity markets. Investing, trading, hedging, arbitrage. Forwards, futures, options, swaps, exotic derivatives. Models of price dynamics, binomial model, introduction to Black-Scholes theory and Monte Carlo simulation. Homework, projects, and guest speakers.
courses.text: Prerequisites: CIV_ENV 205-0 , IEMS 302-0 , IEMS 303-0 or equivalents, or consent of instructor.

courses.title: Supply Chain Modeling and Analysis
courses.desc: Application and development of mathematical modeling tools for the analysis of strategic, tactical, and operational supply-chain problems, including facility location, customer assignment, vehicle routing, and inventory management. Related topics including the role of information and decision support systems in supply chains. Homework, exams, and project.
courses.text: Prerequisite: IEMS 313-0 .

courses.title: Operations Engineering and Management
courses.desc: Applications of operations research methods in managing and control of operations processes in manufacturing and service systems: including operations strategy; process-flow analysis; forecasting; capacity management; variability analysis; flow time and inventory management; flexible operations; lean operations; and production and workforce scheduling in manufacturing and service systems. Case studies, homework, and exams.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 302-0 ; IEMS 310-0 or IEMS 313-0 .

courses.title: Service Engineering and Management
courses.desc: Exploration of service industries: cost-reduction and service-enhancement models, location planning, workforce scheduling, yield management, queuing analysis, and call-center management.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 313-0 , IEMS 315-0 .

courses.title: Introduction to Health Systems Management
courses.desc: Health systems, lean concepts, patient-flow analysis, inference, and data-driven knowledge generation, decisions, and change. Forecasting, operations, and optimization of health resources.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 303-0 , IEMS 313-0 .

courses.title: Client Project Challenge with AI
courses.desc: Open-ended client projects involving application of AI-enabled decision-making techniques to complex data analysis and decision problems. Typically taken at the end of junior year or at the start of senior year. Closed to seniors in spring quarter.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 294-0 , 302-0 , 303-0 , 304-0 , 313-0 ; IEMS 350-0 or IEMS 351-0 or IEMS 352-0 . May not receive credit for both IEMS 392-0 and IEMS 394-0 .

courses.title: Industrial Engineering Client Project Challenge
courses.desc: Open-ended client projects involving application of operations research techniques to complex data analysis and decision problems. Typically taken at the end of junior year or at the start of senior year. Closed to seniors in spring quarter.
courses.text: Prerequisites: IEMS 294-0 , 302-0 , 303-0 , 304-0 , 313-0 ; IEMS 350-0 or IEMS 351-0 or IEMS 352-0 . Antirequisite: May not receive credit for both IEMS 392-0 and IEMS 394-0 .

courses.title: Special Topics in Industrial Engineering
courses.desc: Topics suggested by students or faculty members and approved by the department.

courses.title: Independent Study in Industrial Engineering
courses.desc: Independent study on an industrial engineering topic supervised by a faculty member.

courses.title: Biomedical Engineering Design
courses.desc: Development of a design project initiated during the previous quarter.
courses.text: Prerequisite: BMD_ENG 390-1 .

courses.title: Probability and Statistics for Chemical Engineering
courses.desc: Introduction to probability theory and statistical methods necessary for analyzing the behavior of processes and experiments. Statistical tests for detecting significant changes in process parameters relevant to engineering problems. Students are encouraged but not required to be familiar with coding prior to taking this course.
courses.text: Prerequisites: MATH 220-1 , 220-2 , 228-1 , 228-2 or equivalent; COMP_SCI 150-0 , GEN_ENG 150, or GEN_ENG 151-0 .

courses.title: Economics and Finance for Engineers
courses.desc: Principles of corporate finance; financial decisions of firms; value; risk and return; investment and capital budgeting decisions under certainty and uncertainty; performance evaluation. May not be taken for credit with or after KELLG_FE 310-0.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 220-1 ; basic understanding of probability and economics recommended.

courses.title: Public Speaking
courses.desc: Theory, composition, delivery, and criticism of public speeches.

courses.title: Theories of Persuasion
courses.desc: Survey of major theories that explain how to change another person's attitudes and behaviors. Applications to persuasion within a variety of contexts, including relationships, organizations, legal campaigns, and the mass culture.

courses.title: Introduction to Computer Programming
courses.desc: Introduction to programming practice using a modern programming language. Analysis and formulation of problems for computer solution. Systematic design, construction, and testing of programs. Substantial programming assignments. Not to be taken for credit with or after COMP_SCI 111-0.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Computer Programming
courses.desc: Fundamental concepts of computer programming with heavy emphasis on design of recursive algorithms and test-driven development. Functional, imperative, and object-oriented programming paradigms. Procedural abstraction, data abstraction, and modularity. Required for the computer science degree.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Programming and Computational Problem Solving
courses.desc: An introduction to Object-oriented programming: focus on Python but including a brief introduction to a statically typed language (e.g. C++). Students will use some approaches from Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning to complete programming assignments. Required for the computer science degree. Students may receive credit for only one of: COMP_SCI 150, GEN_ENG 150, and GEN_ENG 151.

courses.title: Applied Data Management
courses.desc: This class offers a hands-on introduction to data representation, data modelling, and the SQL language for accessing and analyzing data in relational databases. Students access and analyze data in real-world large-scale databases from the public domain. Not for computer science or computer engineering degree candidates.
courses.text: Prerequisites: COMP_SCI 150 or GEN_ENG 150 or GEN_ENG 151.

courses.title: Design Thinking and Communication
courses.desc: Integrated introduction to the user-centered design process and technical communication. Students will address challenges proposed by project partners by identifying unmet needs, conducting research, generating and evaluating potential solutions, and finally, presenting a final design concept with supporting documentation. Students also enhance their abilities in equitable teamwork, project management, fabrication skills, and producing written, oral, graphical, and interpersonal communication. One lecture, two section meetings, and lab. Co-registration with ENGLISH 106-1 required. Primarily intended for first-year engineering students.
courses.text: Prerequisite: Reserved for McCormick students only.

courses.title: Design Thinking and Communication
courses.desc: Integrated iteration on the user-centered design process and technical communication. This course will build on the learning objectives from DTC-1 while adding more focus on ethics in design and communication, equitable distribution of teamwork, project management, documenting and communicating progress, and exploring a wider variety of project topics. One lecture, two section meetings, and lab. Co-registration with ENGLISH 106-2 required. Primarily intended for first-year engineering students.
courses.text: Prerequisite: DSGN 106-1 .

courses.title: Writing in Special Contexts
courses.desc: Introduction to expository writing similar to ENGLISH 105-0 but paired with a course in another discipline.

courses.title: Writing in Special Contexts
courses.desc: Introduction to expository writing similar to ENGLISH 105-0 but paired with a course in another discipline.

courses.title: Topics in Literature and Ethics
courses.desc: Although content varies depending on the course topic, all versions of this course explore literary texts that emerge from, and speak back to, ethical and/or religious traditions. Suitable for majors and non-majors. No prior knowledge of the field is expected. May be repeated for credit with a different topic.

courses.title: Principles of Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: This course serves as the foundational course for the undergraduate minor in entrepreneurship. This survey-style course is a good choice for students who wish to familiarize themselves with the world of entrepreneurship. Students will learn to think like entrepreneurs and will be introduced to key topics relevant to entrepreneurship, including customer discovery, finance, and marketing. They will also learn how to understand and perform analyses of a broad range of entrepreneurial activities related to different applications of entrepreneurship. Taught with IEMS 225-0; may not receive credit for both courses.

courses.title: Engineering Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: The goal of the course is to introduce students to innovation-driven entrepreneurship, a process by which emergent technology serves as the catalyst for new venture formation. This course challenges student teams to develop strategies for commercializing cutting-edge technologies. Each year, the course focuses on a significant innovation space. Taught with IEMS 325-0; may not receive credit for both courses.
courses.text: Prerequisite: ENTREP 330-1 .

courses.title: Startup Accounting and Finance
courses.desc: This course meets a core requirement for the Farley undergraduate minor in entrepreneurship. This course teaches students foundational accounting principles and how to manage the finances of small and early-stage businesses. Students will work in teams on projects driven by case studies and will immediately be able to apply their learnings to their own startup projects.

courses.title: Leadership, Ethics, and You
courses.desc: This class is designed for students who want to explore how ethics and integrity are tied to leadership, and how developing leadership skills can contribute to students' future successes in both entrepreneurial endeavors and more traditional careers.

courses.title: Tech Ethics and Business Integrity
courses.desc: This course will explore the unique ethical challenges that face the technology industry, utilizing recent and historical case studies. Students will be challenged to think about what it means to run a business with integrity by examining common issues within the workplace as well as the responsibility that businesses have to customers. Data privacy abuses, sexual misconduct, and corporate greed, among many other topics, will be addressed.

courses.title: Elementary Applied Linear Algebra
courses.desc: Basic linear algebra methods including basic matrix/vector operations, solution of linear systems of equations, eigenvalues, and singular values. Focus will be on applications of the methods on a range of engineering topics including: least squares and data fitting, game theory, graph theory, principal component analysis, linear programming, and other related engineering topics.

courses.title: Programming for Engineers
courses.desc: Object-Oriented Programming including Programming Basics (Data abstraction, Simple procedures, Primitive data), Procedural Programming Fundamentals (Conditional Execution, Iteration, Recursion, Modularity and Procedural abstraction, Composite data - lists, dictionaries), and Object-Oriented Principles (Composite data -classes, Encapsulation, Inheritance). Students may receive credit for only one of: COMP_SCI 150, GEN_ENG 150, and GEN_ENG 151.

courses.title: Honors Programming for Engineers
courses.desc: Object-Oriented Programming including Programming Basics (Data abstraction, Simple procedures, Primitive data), Procedural Programming Fundamentals (Conditional Execution, Iteration, Recursion, Modularity and Procedural abstraction, Composite data - lists, dictionaries), and Object-Oriented Principles (Composite data -classes, Encapsulation, Inheritance). The honors section will include students who received a 4 or 5 on AP CS A.
courses.text: Prerequisite: COMP_SCI 1CA or instructor permission. Students may not receive credit for both GEN_ENG 151-0 and COMP_SCI 150-0 or GEN_ENG 150-0 .

courses.title: Engineering Analysis I
courses.desc: Introduction to linear algebra from computational, mathematical, and applications viewpoints. Computational methods using a higher-level software package such as MATLAB.

courses.title: Honor Engineering Analysis
courses.desc: Covers topics addressed in GEN_ENG 205-1 at a deeper level. Intended for students with demonstrated strength in mathematics, computer programming, and/or physics.
courses.text: Prerequisite: consent of instructor.

courses.title: Probability and Statistics for Engineers
courses.desc: Collecting, summarizing and displaying data. An introduction to probability theory and its applications. Conditional probabilities and expected values. Random variables and distributions. Drawing conclusions and making decisions using data: confidence intervals, hypotheses testing, comparison tests, regression, and correlation.
courses.text: Prerequisites: GEN_ENG 150 or GEN_ENG 151, MATH 220-2 . You may not enroll in both GEN_ENG 231-0 and GEN_ENG 241-0 during initial registration. This restriction will be removed after the initial registration period if capacity allows.

courses.title: Linear Algebra for Engineers
courses.desc: Solving linear systems of equations and LU factorization. Matrix/vector operations and algebra. Vector spaces and bases. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Orthogonality, solution of least squares, and QR factorization. Singular values, singular value decomposition. Applications in science and engineering.
courses.text: Prerequisites: GEN_ENG 150 or 151, MATH 220-2 . You may not enroll in both GEN_ENG 231-0 and GEN_ENG 241-0 during initial registration. This restriction will be removed after the initial registration period if capacity allows.

courses.title: Single-Variable Calculus with Precalculus
courses.desc: Extreme value theorem, mean value theorem, and curve-sketching. Related rates. Optimization. Transcendental and inverse functions. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 218-2 and any of MATH 211-0, MATH 212-0 (former), MATH 220-0 (former), or MATH 220-1.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 218-1 or consent of the department.

courses.title: Single-Variable Differential Calculus
courses.desc: Limits. Differentiation. Linear approximation and related rates. Extreme value theorem, mean value theorem, and curve-sketching. Optimization. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 220-1 and any of MATH 211-0, MATH 212-0 (former), MATH 213-0 (former), MATH 218-1, MATH 218-2, or MATH 220-0 (former).

courses.title: Single-Variable Integral Calculus
courses.desc: Definite integrals, antiderivatives, and the fundamental theorem of calculus. Transcendental and inverse functions. Areas and volumes. Techniques of integration, numerical integration, and improper integrals. First-order linear and separable ordinary differential equations. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 220-2 and any of MATH 213-0 (former), MATH 214-0 (former), MATH 218-3, or MATH 224-0 (former).
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 218-2 or MATH 220-0 (former) or MATH 220-1 .

courses.title: Multivariable Differential Calculus for Engineering
courses.desc: Vectors, vector functions, partial derivatives, Taylor polynomials, and optimization. Emphasis on engineering applications. For McCormick School of Engineering students only. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 228-1 and any of MATH 230-0 (former), MATH 230-1, MATH 281-1, MATH 285-2, MATH 290-2, MATH 291-2, or ES_APPM 252-1.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 218-3 or MATH 214-0 (former) or MATH 220-2 or MATH 224-0 (former).

courses.title: Multivariable Integral Calculus for Engineering
courses.desc: Multiple integration: double integrals, triple integrals, and change of variables. Vector calculus: vector fields, line integrals, surface integrals, curl and divergence, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem. Emphasis on engineering applications. For McCormick School of Engineering students only. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 228-2 and any of MATH 230-2, MATH 234-0 (former), MATH 281-2, MATH 285-3, MATH 290-3, MATH 291-3, or ES_APPM 252-2.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 228-1 or MATH 230-0 (former) or MATH 230-1 or MATH 281-1 or MATH 285-2 or MATH 290-2 or MATH 291-2 or ES_APPM 252-1 .

courses.title: Linear Algebra
courses.desc: Elementary linear algebra: systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, subspaces, determinants, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and orthogonality. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 240-0 and any of MATH 281-3, MATH 285-1, MATH 290-1, MATH 291-1, GEN_ENG 205-1, or GEN_ENG 206-1.
courses.text: Prerequisite: MATH 230-1 or MATH 230-0 (former) or MATH 281-1 or ES_APPM 252-1 .

courses.title: Probability and Statistics for Econometrics
courses.desc: Introduction to probability theory and statistical methods, including properties of probability distributions, sampling distributions, parameter estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. For students planning to take ECON 381-1. Students may not receive credit for both MATH 314-0 and any of MATH 310-1, MATH 311-1, MATH 385-0, STAT 320-1, STAT 383-0, IEMS 302-0, or ELEC_ENG 302-0. Prerequisite or corequisite: MATH 226-0 or MATH 281-2; and MATH 228-2 or MATH 230-2 or MATH 234-0 (former), or MATH 281-2 or MATH 285-3 or MATH 290-3 or MATH 291-3 or ES_APPM 252-2.

courses.title: Analysis and Performance of Text
courses.desc: This course studies texts, broadly defined and situated, through performance. Students explore how performance helps the performer and audience interpret a text, as well as express challenging political and personal themes. They examine the ways performance illuminates and draws out deeper understandings of social relations through embodied praxis.

courses.title: Performance Culture and Communication
courses.desc: Explores how live performance and dramatic forms of communication are methods used to examine social behavior and cultural expressions.

courses.title: Introduction to Critical Theory
courses.desc: Crisis, criticism, and critique in philosophical, political, and cultural contexts. Focus on the philosophical aspects of critical theory with reference to social conditions and art, literary, and/or political forms. COMP_LIT 207-0 and PHIL 220-0 are taught together; may not receive credit for both courses.

courses.title: Minds and Machines
courses.desc: Introductory course addressing philosophical issues arising from the study of intelligence, including the possibility of machine intelligence and its relevance to the study of human intelligence.

courses.title: Introduction to Moral Philosophy
courses.desc: Overview of some of the main ideas and most influential writings of moral philosophy.

courses.title: Ethical Problems and Public Issues
courses.desc: Analysis of such controversial issues as the death penalty, abortion, euthanasia, sexual morality, economic justice and welfare, pornography and censorship, discrimination and preferential treatment, the environment, and world hunger.

courses.title: Bioethics
courses.desc: Ethical analysis of a variety of issues such as the human genome project, genetic therapy, cloning and stem cell transplantation, human and animal research, reproductive technologies, and the allocation of resources.

courses.title: Scientific Method in the Social Sciences
courses.desc: Analysis of the philosophical foundations of social inquiry with reference to selected problems, thinkers, and schools, both classical and modern.

courses.title: Business and Professional Ethics
courses.desc: Application of ethical theories (Kantianism, utilitarianism, etc.) in a commercial setting. Topics include social responsibilities of corporations, public regulation, moral limits of marketing (e.g., marketing to children, noxious products), social justice versus fair compensation.

courses.title: General Physics
courses.desc: Calculus-based physics for science and engineering majors and premedical students. Mechanics. Must be taken concurrently with PHYSICS 136-1.
courses.text: Prerequisites: MATH 220-1 , MATH 220-2 ; MATH 230-1 OR MATH 290-1 OR MATH 291-1 (may be taken concurrently).

courses.title: Integrity and the Politics of Corruption
courses.desc: This seminar delves into fraught political problems revolving around corruption and abuse of power. To tackle these problems, we examine two ideas related to "the people." First, the people as the owner of public property stolen by corrupt politicians. Second, the people as an agent with its own moral integrity. Both ideas combine abstract philosophy with concrete politics.

courses.title: Engineering Improv: From Allowing to Application
courses.desc: Start anywhere, remember you are not the most important person in the scene, and say yes. Through these and other improv techniques, students learn to tackle unexpected obstacles, building skills that can be leveraged in both academic and non-academic contexts to face challenges with resilience.
